overview: This record represents the eighteenth-century Republic of Geneva, a small state centered on the city at the Rhône’s outlet from Lake Geneva. Its imported 1700 to 1800 interval is only a map window: French annexation ended the republic’s independence in 1798. The outline is approximate and should not be read as the borders of the larger Swiss canton created later.

periods.title: The old republic
periods.summary: Political privileges coexisted with a prosperous craft economy.

periods.title: Revolution and a constitution
periods.summary: Revolution changed the government and the 1794 constitution expanded political participation.

periods.title: French administration
periods.summary: French annexation replaced the republic’s councils.

sections.title: Who belonged, and who had a vote?

items.text: Living and working in Geneva did not automatically bring political rights. Foreign residents called habitants and their locally born descendants, the natifs, were excluded from political participation and faced economic restrictions. Many worked in crafts linked to watchmaking. A family could help make the city prosperous while remaining shut out of its government.

Geneva’s famous Fabrique was a network of small watchmaking and related workshops. The word sounds like one enormous factory, but work was distributed among many skilled hands. The products traveled abroad through commercial connections in cities such as Paris, London and Amsterdam. A small workshop could therefore be part of a much bigger trading world.

Printed cotton fabrics known as indiennes belonged to another important industry. Unlike the watch trades’ small workshops, these goods were produced in larger manufactories. Eighteenth-century Geneva supported different kinds of working environments at the same time; a cloth worker and a watchmaker did not necessarily experience the same working day.

In the early 1700s, engineer Joseph Abeille installed a pumping system that initially supplied seven public fountains. It drew on the lake and Rhône water system. Public fountains made water available through shared infrastructure, rather than a tap in every kitchen. The work of supplying a city involved pumps and maintenance as well as the river itself.

Smallpox threatened children and could kill or permanently scar survivors. In eighteenth-century Geneva, families and doctors debated inoculation, an earlier practice distinct from modern vaccination. It could protect against later disease but could itself cause serious illness. Parents therefore faced a difficult decision, not the effortless acceptance sometimes suggested by stories of scientific progress.

In 1751, hospital directors arranged inoculations for children dependent on the institution. Historians point out that these children were unable to object. Wealthier families could seek private arrangements and pay for care. The records show how medical experimentation and access to care were shaped by children’s unequal power and circumstances.

Théodore Tronchin introduced theoretical medical lessons and practical anatomy demonstrations at Geneva’s Academy in 1754. His honorary chair was short-lived. Students could encounter medical teaching, but Geneva did not yet possess the modern medical faculty that would be established in the nineteenth century.

Horace-Bénédict de Saussure and instrument maker Jaques Paul used a hair’s response to dampness to measure humidity. The prepared hair changed length as conditions changed, moving a pointer on a scale. Building the mechanism required careful craft as well as scientific ideas. A single hair could have a surprisingly demanding laboratory job.

A surviving late-eighteenth-century hygrometer bears the French inscription “Paul à Genève”, meaning “Paul in Geneva.” The UNIL-EPFL collection catalogs it as instrument 603.1018, dated 1783 to 1800. This small maker’s signature is an attested sample of written language on a working scientific object. It names the workshop’s maker and city, rather than a king.

sections.title: Ideas, rights and the republic’s ending

items.text: Geneva celebrated learning but also censored ideas. On 19 June 1762, its authorities ordered Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s Emile and The Social Contract to be torn and burned outside the city hall. A book discussing education or government could become a political event. Rousseau’s connection to Geneva did not shield his books from its magistrates.

The constitution of 1794 introduced juries and separated governmental powers. Its language of popular sovereignty did not include everyone: citizenship remained limited to Protestant men. The reforms changed important rules of justice while leaving exclusions in place, a distinction that matters when reading the period’s promises of equality.

French troops entered Geneva in April 1798, and the republic’s councils were abolished. Geneva became the administrative center of the French department of Léman. The republic was restored at the end of 1813, and Geneva joined the Swiss Confederation in 1815. Those later changes explain how the former independent city became a Swiss canton.

ending.text: French military occupation and annexation ended the republic’s independence in 1798. Geneva regained a republican government in 1813 and became a Swiss canton in 1815; the city and its communities continued through those changes.
